summary: Records the threats against the Domain Name System that DNSSEC is meant to protect against, something that was never written down while DNSSEC was being developed. It helps judge whether DNSSEC actually meets its goals and what it leaves unaddressed.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lists ways attackers can mislead DNS resolvers or disrupt name lookups. It explains which of these threats DNSSEC can address and which remain.

questions: what is a name chaining attack
subtitle: A threat analysis of DNS and an assessment of which attacks the DNS Security Extensions can address.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC was developed without a detailed, written list of the threats it was meant to address. This made it difficult to judge whether its design met its goals.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes DNS threats, including interception, guessing, name chaining, untrusted servers, denial of service, and attacks involving absent names and wildcards. It discusses how DNSSEC and related mechanisms help or fall short.
tldr.outcome: The authors conclude that DNSSEC addresses real threats and is worth deploying, but it does not prevent every attack and has operational costs and weaknesses.

today: RFC 3833 is an Informational RFC published in August 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records a threat analysis and does not specify a DNS protocol.

sections.title: DNSSEC Goals and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC records the goals chosen for DNSSEC: data integrity and data-origin authentication. The design team treated DNS data as public, so hiding it was out of scope; authenticating clients and servers for access control was also out of scope. Backward compatibility with insecure DNS was an explicit requirement.

This document assumes readers already know DNS and DNSSEC. It uses DNSSEC for the core hierarchical public-key and signature mechanism, while treating TKEY and TSIG as separate mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC aims to show that DNS data is unchanged and came from the expected source. It does not aim to hide DNS data or authenticate clients for access control.

sections.title: Interception, Guessing and Trusted Servers
sections.content:
An attacker who intercepts DNS traffic can send a forged reply before the real one. DNS usually sends a query or reply in one unsigned, unencrypted UDP packet. Guessing the DNS identifier and client port can also help inject a false response, especially when the resolver's query or port is predictable.

A resolver may also receive wrong answers from a server it chose to trust. DNSSEC signature checking can detect forged data when the resolver performs the checks itself. TSIG can protect communication with a chosen server, but does not make that server trustworthy. DNSSEC does not protect the DNS message header.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker may forge a reply on the network, guess which reply a resolver expects, or operate a server that gives wrong answers. A resolver that checks DNSSEC signatures can detect many forged answers, but DNSSEC does not protect the message header.

sections.title: Name Chaining, Missing Records and Wildcards
sections.content:
Name chaining is a form of cache poisoning in which records containing DNS names can direct later lookups. CNAME, NS, and DNAME records can redirect a query; MX and SRV records can lead to further lookups. The RFC says DNSSEC can defend against most of these attacks by letting resolvers check that data was signed by the delegated authority. Glue records are not covered by DNSSEC signatures.

Authenticated denial helps a resolver determine whether a name or record type exists, which matters when an attacker removes records. Wildcard answers also need proof that the wildcard exists and that no existing record makes it inapplicable. DNSSEC includes mechanisms for checking wildcard expansion.
sections.plainLanguage: Some DNS records can send a later lookup to another name, so false records can redirect a resolver. DNSSEC can check who signed records and can help verify that a name or record is absent, though glue records are not covered.

sections.title: Denial of Service and DNSSEC Weaknesses
sections.content:
DNSSEC does not stop denial-of-service attacks, and signature checking can increase resolver work and the number of messages needed for an answer. DNS replies are often larger than queries, and DNSSEC increases response size, so DNS servers can remain useful as denial-of-service amplifiers.

The RFC also lists DNSSEC complexity, configuration errors, expired keys, increased delay, dependence on a hierarchical trust model, difficult root-key rollover, and a need for loose clock synchronization. Wildcard handling adds complexity, and a resolver must be configured to know which records it expects to be signed.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC adds checks but does not prevent a flood of traffic from stopping a service. It also adds work, delay, configuration demands, and dependence on a chain of trusted keys and reasonably aligned clocks.

sections.title: Future Work and Conclusion
sections.content:
The RFC identifies further work on interactions with other protocols, secure dynamic updates, and secure zone replication. For a secure dynamic update, a zone-signing key must be available to the updating client or the name server. For zone transfers, TSIG protects the channel, but DNSSEC does not provide object security for complete zones containing unsigned delegation data.

The authors conclude that DNSSEC appears to solve a set of problems that need solving and is worth deploying. They also state that it helps with some, but not all, known DNS threats.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC identifies open questions about changing and copying signed DNS zones. Its conclusion is that DNSSEC helps against important threats, but does not solve every DNS security problem.
